speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the view of some Singaporeans and healthcare workers I have spoken to, these efforts are not yet fighting-fit to take on some of the big health challenges of the near future and are already not delivering the health outcomes that we could be achieving for a well-developed nation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By preventive health efforts here, I mean our policies and programmes for reducing the incidence of chronic disease conditions like diabetes, hypertension and so on, as well as our policies to move Singaporeans towards better health outcomes in general.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this speech, I will detail proposals fitting into three overall thrusts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One, we should adopt an outcomes-focused approach that is long term but given tough regular reviews.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two, we should reward the good health choices of individuals, especially at-risk groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And three, we should use highly targeted strategies that nudge healthcare providers and leverage data towards better health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, first, let us take stock of our preventive health efforts and the huge health problems that we face.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are many worthy programmes that have been undertaken.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, in public discussions of what the Government does to nudge Singapore towards living healthier lifestyles, the National Steps Challenge is often mentioned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, what is the picture that emerges when we look at indicators of chronic conditions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We find that the incidence of certain dangerous chronic conditions has increased steadily in recent decades.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are we in danger of racking up an "A" grade for effort but a "C" grade for outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, Singapore was number two in the world in diabetes prevalence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, one in four Singaporeans aged 40 and above has at least one chronic disease.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The proportion of older adults with three or more chronic diseases nearly doubled from 2009 to 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2017 MOH study showed that Singaporeans may have a longer life expectancy today but do not necessarily enjoy a better quality of health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans born in 2017 are expected to spend on average 1.5 more years in poor health compared to those born in 1990 and this refers to the years spent on average in poor health, alive but in poor health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, an HPB expert noted that if obesity is not effectively curbed, Singapore could hit obesity rates of 15% in just seven years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That was the point at which obesity increased rapidly in the United States where it is now considered an epidemic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: According to a report by The Economist, cardiovascular diseases contribute to approximately one in three deaths in Singapore and levy about US$11 billion in costs on individuals, their households and the public finances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Modifiable risk factors for CVD, such as smoking and cholesterol levels, account for 60% of these costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In short, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we have a very big problem that needs to be tackled now with new thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My first recommendation is that the Government should focus more clearly on outputs and outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should set clear goals for outputs like the proportion of persons exercising regularly, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should also state clear short- and medium-term targets for lowering chronic disease incidence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We cannot succeed if we do not define what success looks like.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Meeting such targets is, of course, dependent on a range of factors and not only Government policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is clear and I do not disagree with this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We cannot, ultimately, micro-manage personal behaviour but we should know what are the short- and medium-term targets for outputs and outcomes that we are aiming at, so that we know when we are away from goodness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is useful to refer to participation rates for programmes and events, the number of app downloads and so on and so forth, but these, Sir, are effort indicators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must not over-emphasise effort indicators in our public communications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Doing well on effort indicators can lull us into a false sense of security and self-congratulation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These determine whether we have won or lost the battle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, during this time, the prevalence of obesity, high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol had risen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some types of efforts may not yield good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One example, HPB's "1 Million kg Challenge" in 2014 set a clear target of a collective weight loss of one million kilogrammes, from at least 300,000 participants over three years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The CEO of HPB has publicly acknowledged that they only managed to lose a few tens of thousands of kilogrammes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is important to draw lessons from such experiences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As an international example for comparison, I will cite the Nordic Plan of Action which sets specific ambitious targets for reducing obesity rates and improving physical activity levels and healthy diets, with a regular monitoring system every two years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While recent results in that part of the world have not been very good, at least there is a robust, transparent system, with targets and monitoring to drive towards the right outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is time to provide serious financial nudges to citizens to encourage healthy behaviours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, we should provide some cash incentives or subsidies for MediShield premiums to those who demonstrate a commitment to healthier behaviours, such as regular screenings or regular exercise, as verified by way of attendance records or wearable technology, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have tried such schemes before, such as Lumihealth, the Apple watch tie-up, but we must put our money where our mouth is to ensure these schemes reach more people, in particular, those who are not yet exercising, eating well or going for their screenings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can use various touch-points, like family doctors in whom many trust deeply, to spread the word.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are examples of health insurers in other countries that provide premium discounts based on the adoption of behaviours that tend to make payouts for medical treatment less likely.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, the US insurance provider Vitality provides premium discounts for members alongside freebies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I realise that this is a significant departure from the current approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Further study should be done before adopting this as a general policy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The approach of testing a major policy through randomised controlled trials was also something I argued for when calling for smaller form class sizes in schools in an Adjournment Motion in 2017 and I have argued for this year as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In its GE 2020 manifesto, the Workers' Party called for making COVID-19 vaccines free, long before they had been successfully launched.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is something that most governments in the world have done, including Singapore's Government, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the principle of making vaccines free can be extended.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Other things being equal, higher vaccination rates have the potential to minimise disease incidence and, hence, reduce public and private expense in healthcare treatment for those diseases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I also called for a bigger role for free vaccines in the public health system, rather than simply allowing MediSave to be used for vaccines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans are reluctant to touch it for something less tangible like a vaccine, fearing that they would need all the MediSave that they can get later in life for actual medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Vaccines have huge public benefits, as we have seen during COVID-19, so the Government should pay for them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2020, the Government announced some improvements to subsidy levels for vaccines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I remember having an exchange in this House with then Senior Parliamentary Secretary Mr Amrin Amin, asking him if the subsidies for vaccines can be pegged to the amount of money the state would save from higher vaccination rates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He replied, saying they were crafting this package and would announce the details in time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is much more that can be done to improve vaccine take-up rates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our take-up rate for flu vaccines, for example, is much lower than it should be, compared to some other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a great deal of suffering and costs involved in treating flu patients who become ill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us start with making flu vaccines free and thus easy to get for key groups like pregnant women, those with chronic health conditions and older folk over 65.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Again, GPs can play a big role in promoting adult vaccination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This reasoning can also be applied to the pneumococcal vaccine.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A healthier population is always worth investing in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Screen for Life (SFL) is a well-intentioned policy, but low take-up rates leave much to improve on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Take-up is notably skewed towards the Chinese community, compared to other ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are worthy efforts, but, clearly, the results still leave room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: HPB should conduct studies into the reasons for low take-up rates despite heavy subsidies for health screening under SFL.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, lower-income constituents I have met will occasionally share that they do not wish to go for health screening as they are daunted by the high cost of treatment, or what they perceive to be the high cost of treatment, if disease is detected.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If those who are most at risk of chronic diseases are not getting screened, this will not only incur greater downstream costs to the individual and the society, but also raise deeper questions about access to basic healthcare for the most vulnerable among us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, for now, I would like to offer some policy suggestions here on raising health screening take-up rates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some insurers, like NTUC Income, reward policyholders who have good health screening results with shopping vouchers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, one in three diabetics, one in four people with hypertension and almost half of those with high cholesterol levels do not know that they have these conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Those who do not know that they have these diseases will push up costs for everyone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have called in a past Parliamentary Question for inclusion of waist circumference measurement in national health screenings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This metric is important in defining obesity risk, rather than over-relying on the Body Mass Index (BMI).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am glad that MOH is moving to implement this and I look forward to seeing more evidence-based inclusions in health screening.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, in nudging individuals towards healthier choices, I think it is important to place special attention on especially vulnerable groups, like the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many lower-income Singaporeans lack the means to purchase and cook healthier foods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When I say this, of course, I do not mean that all healthy foods are costly, but many healthy food decisions are more expensive, complicated or time-consuming.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In providing aid to lower-income families, can some of our aid be provided in the form of highly frictionless digital currency earmarked for the purchase of healthier food products with, for example, less saturated fat and sugar?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could also focus on unprocessed foods like raw meat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A digital currency would be easily programmable and could be updated monthly to reflect inflation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With RFID technology in supermarkets and grocery chains, this should not be too difficult to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the past, we have tried vouchers and other similar programmes, but if we could have a regular provision of frictionless aid, this would act as a much stronger nudge to eat healthily at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our preventive health programmes tend to place personal responsibility on individuals to take charge of their health and lead healthy lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, we have a collective responsibility to ensure the less privileged among us also have access to healthy lifestyle habits and are supported in that direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Health is a critical dimension in improving lives and livelihoods for poorer Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Though it should be said that similar statistics can be found in other developed countries, at the 2021 Committee of Supply, then Health Minister Gan Kim Yong, remarked that MOH paid special attention to lower-income households, including their preventive health needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With more data, we can devise better programmes to nudge those on lower-incomes towards better health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to talk about incentives for healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we think of alternative models where there is a degree of incentivisation based on the success of the healthcare provider in nudging patients towards better health outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other words, instead of paying providers just for treating the sick, can we pay them in part, at least, for encouraging their patients not to get sick in the first place?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The notion is not as utopian as it seems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A few healthcare systems in the world are inching towards that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, Kaiser Permanente in California is well-regarded as a provider of high-quality, efficient and affordable integrated care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is three separate entities: a health plan that bears insurance risk, medical groups of physicians and the hospital system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The financial incentive there is to provide a high-quality continuum of care and maximise population health, rather than profiting from a high volume of compensable services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we thus remodel our system of healthcare providers to incorporate incentives for effective preventive health work with patients, rather than just rely on compensation to the healthcare provider being linked only to the performance of treatments and tests?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One other specific example would be to empower healthcare providers with inter-operable IT systems that can flag out if a patient has not got a mammogram or a blood screening recently and direct the patient to get that done while they are visiting for something else entirely.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would be the medical equivalent of a no-wrong-door approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moving towards such an alternative system of compensation for healthcare providers is, indeed, a very big, some would say, radical idea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As always, piloting randomised controlled trials are all advisable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Sir, I would argue that we should make health data available more quickly and in more granular detail regarding chronic conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Much of the data on disease incidence is not published so frequently and after a significant time lag from data collection.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: COVID-19 has shown that we can publish data on healthcare metrics practically in real time when the political will is there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It will help Members to know where there are concentrations of particular health issues, with a purpose of raising relevant talking points when we meet constituents and perhaps organising relevant ground events such as talks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, can we nudge patients to provide permission for data-sharing across healthcare providers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would enable medical professionals to reduce duplication of tests and get a more holistic picture of every patient's health situation at any time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The US NPO Kaiser Permanente, again, is widely recognised as having pioneered some world-class IT systems that help doctors do just that, suggesting to doctors that patients may have a certain condition in some cases, in the same way that Amazon prompts buyers by saying those who bought this book also liked this other book.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That would mean more human suffering and more pressure on our fiscal resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When the costs of failing are socialised, as it is in this preventive health war, stronger action is justified.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The rewards for early, bold, decisive action can be tremendous.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our children and grandchildren will thank us for taking those actions today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are useful improvements that MOH will consider, but I would not describe them as a rethink of preventive health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, improving preventive health has been on the agenda of MOH for many years now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This, in fact, set the stage for the formation of Primary Care Networks (PCN) to strengthen the doctor-patient relationship in the management of chronic diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) was also enhanced to support the financing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2017, MOH announced our "three Beyonds" strategy: Beyond healthcare to health; Beyond hospital to community; and Beyond quality to value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong, in his Committee of Supply 2017 speech, emphasised the importance of focusing on early interventions and healthy lifestyle choices to go "Beyond Healthcare to Health".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And he further gave the example of how one front of the war on diabetes would be fought via healthy living and prevention, encouraging the population to stay active and eat healthy to reduce the risk of diabetes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the MOH Workplan Seminar last year – which was his first public speech as Minister for Health – Minister Ong Ye Kung focused his speech on preventive care, emphasising how interventions should move and have moved upstream to tackle lifestyle risk factors for chronic diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In comments made during the Ministerial panel on Primary Care at the session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific held in October 2021, Minister Ong also shared that MOH was looking to change the system focus from acute hospital care back to preventive care provided in the community and primary care settings, which would result in a very good quality system that is also sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since then, we have been engaged in dialogues and in-depth discussions with our GP leaders and many in our Healthcare Cluster leadership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of the things we discussed is on the possibility of a capitation model, to transform our primary care providers' way of engaging with our patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, MOH's big push to revamp preventive care in recent months is really no big secret.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And we thank Mr Leon Perera for weighing in, and supporting this move, including providing some useful suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over the weekend, in fact, at the topping-out ceremony of the Woodlands Health Campus, Minister Ong Ye Kung said that he would be announcing a national programme focusing on preventive care at the coming Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I hope Mr Leon Perera and the Workers' Party Members will give it their full support at the Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Leon Perera suggested more subsidies and incentives to promote screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: His underlying assumption is that if we make things cheaper, in fact, make it free, the take-up rate will improve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But actually, having sat across the table with many patients, advising them on health screening, in preventive health, the hardest hurdle to overcome is the mindset and health beliefs of the individual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We all know what is good for us, health-wise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Every doctor counsels and wants his patients to go and do the right things for his own health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But, alas, in real life, changing mindset and health-seeking beliefs is not something that policy or clinical protocols alone can change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Eligible individuals pay no more than $5 for screening under SFL and MediSave can be used for approved screenings, including colonoscopy screening for colon cancer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This illustrates the point that despite efforts to reduce the cost barrier to screening, more still needs to be done to address the individual’s perceptions, their barriers, their fears, to undergo screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have to do more to nudge them to undertake screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Vaccination is an important component of preventive health interventions, a point that Mr Leon Perera also made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, Mr Leon Perera's call for free vaccination is already, in effect, being done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: All adult Singaporeans are eligible for means-tested subsidies at both CHAS GP clinics and polyclinics for recommended vaccinations under the the National Adult Immunisation Schedule (NAIS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MediSave can also be used for any approved NAIS vaccinations, which means that co-payment could, in fact, be zero.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And this includes influenza vaccination for our elderly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH also uses other touchpoints to increase adoption of these important vaccinations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is in addition to fully subsidised vaccinations provided as part of the immunisation schedule delivered in schools via HPB's School Health Service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH has also been working with our primary care partners to increase vaccination uptake, especially among seniors, for influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Seniors are also able to learn more about the importance of vaccinations through interactive health workshops conducted within the community and through online platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Tackling preventive health requires an "integrated" as well as a "life-course" approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over the years, we have built a strong foundation in various key domains across different agencies: health promotion under HPB, health screening and chronic disease management by our GP clinics and polyclinics as well as our Healthcare Clusters, promoting sports and active lifestyle by Active SG and encouraging citizens to remain active in our Community Clubs and interest groups  Having built up all these key pieces, we now move to enhance the delivery of evidence-based preventive health to the population by integrating them together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, the "Health Up!" initiative in Tampines, an initiative led by SingHealth polyclinics, in partnership with agencies, such as HPB, Changi General Hospital, Tampines GRC and SportSG, is a very good example of how the different stakeholders have come together to provide a holistic and structured health journey for residents by increasing awareness of healthy lifestyle habits and promoting appropriate screening for disease.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With this integrative approach, a resident who undergoes health screening by the GP to determine the health parameters that needed improvement – could be his BMI, could be his blood control targets – can be subsequently assessed by a fitness coach under Active SG to customise a fitness regime targeting these particular goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A structured exercise regime which also connects the resident with the Community Sports Club builds a network of peer support, friendships, peer groups, that eventually enables a sustained active lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, a Care Coordinator from Changi General Hospital serves as an "account manager" to help coordinate the health journey of the participant and helps transmit data, helps to coordinate the programme between the GP, the coach and the dietician.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This entire process will be data-driven such that the GPs and the coaches have a shared view of the progress, participation and target goals that the individual has achieved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Suitable incentives and gamification can eventually be built into this process to further encourage and ingrain healthier habits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The "Health Up!" integrated approach aims to build an ecosystem within the community and centre around the individual so that this, hopefully, provides stronger support to encourage more upstream preventive health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH is also moving upstream to promote healthy lifestyle by adopting a life-course approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Healthy habits start young – prevention is better than cure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: HPB works with MOE and the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) to provide school health promotion initiatives and healthier food options for students in preschools and our schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For the general adult population, our health promotion efforts include public education to increase health literacy and awareness of modifiable lifestyle risk factors for chronic diseases with health messages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with MOM and other partners, HPB also aims to improve the health of working adults by transforming workplace clusters into Healthy Workplace Ecosystems (HWEs) through partnering developers and key industry partners to deliver customised programmes to mature workers in seven priority sectors and the gig economy workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Programmes are also offered directly to companies, including SMEs and mid- to large-sized companies and organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, doctors are supported by the National Electronic Health Records to access their patients' records for patient management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singaporeans have access to own consolidated health records and eligibility for screening subsidies through Health Hub to empower self-management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will also certainly leverage on technology and analytics to transform citizens' experience in health promotion programmes, moving from a "one-size-fits-all" approach to a more precise and personalised approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: LumiHealth, an example that the Member has quoted, was launched in 2020, is one such intervention that has empowered individuals to take charge of their health through precise and personalised insights and recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These reports are actually publicly available via the MOH website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There is a need to double up the preventive health efforts as we seek to regain the momentum and improvements that were lost due to the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There is an urgent need for the population to take action and participate in improving their health as we emerge from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
